strengths: The target task and range of applicability for the proposed method are clearly articulated, and the core idea ("retroactive" or "interaction-first" labeling) is very clever.
The empirical results from the fine-tuning experiments seem reasonably good overall.

Effort has been put into making the work reproducible – the prompts used for each system component are available in the appendix, which helps understand the work even where descriptions in the paper could be clearer.
The writing is, on balance, reasonably clear and free from distracting problems related to grammar or diction.
The idea could be broadly useful for synthetic data generation in many contexts.
The paper is easy to follow and overall does a decent job at grounding different things.
The paper releases the demonstrations they have collected using the proposed approach (although with a different LM than used for the paper).
Compared to the baseline methods (Zero-Shot, SFT(instruction-first), SFT(NNetnav+Distil.)), NNetnav successfully improves the performance on MiniWoB++ and WebArena.
Proposes a method for generating synthetic trajectories using LLM exploration and hindsight relabeling for web applications.
Demonstrates that training on these trajectories leads to better performance compared to instruction-first trajectories and zero-shot baselines on WebArena.
Synthetic data generation without human annotation for improving LLM agents on the web is an important problem, and well motivated in the paper.
weaknesses: Clarity issues: the introduction's discussion of the pruning approach is unclear; trajectory prefixes as the basic unit of labeling is not obvious; need to clarify that elements of observation and action spaces have string representations; the term "plausible" is undefined and not quantified; lack of direct evaluation of instruction quality.

Notation issues: sections 2 and 3 use textbook RL notation that is inconsistent with the task; unclear whether \pi is a distribution over actions or strings; unclear definition of \mathcal{A} (finite set of actions vs larger LLM output set); need to specify whether policies work with probabilities or strings and the nature of the string set.

Reward model confusion: paper seems to use binary rewards (line 199) which is inconsistent with prompts for s_{LM}; later clarification but reuse of notation for binary and graded rewards is confusing.
Results concerns: cross-website generalization appears weak; tables lack units and clear captions; significance of small improvements (e.g., 0.06 and 0.13) is unclear without knowing reward scale.
NNetNav-6k dataset usage is unclear; it is not evident whether the dataset was used beyond release, no assessment of its quality, and it does not appear to be used for fine-tuning models.
The claim that GPT-4o and Llama-3 have "similar quality" lacks rigorous justification.
The assumption that web browsing is deterministic is questionable.
The overall methodological contribution seems quite heuristic driven; reliance on \pi_explore which is similar to the zero-shot baseline may fail in challenging environments.
Other parts of the algorithm are heuristic driven, such as LM summarization of state changes (\delta_t), which can be noisy and may hinder scalability.
Lack of a baseline using limited human demonstrations, which could provide higher-quality data and improve \pi_explore.

The authors collected and released a larger set of demonstrations but only used a smaller subset for training; they should explore using all demonstrations and examine performance scaling with more demos.
The ablation baseline (instructions-only) is competitive with the proposed approach, yet the authors did not further explore or improve this baseline nor analyze differences in rollouts.
The proposed pipeline is quite similar to BAGEL (Murty et al., 2024), limiting novelty.

It is unclear whether the achieved performance is meaningful to the community; reported success rates (e.g., 48% on MiniWoB, 7.2% on WebArena) do not represent progress compared to existing benchmarks.
The effectiveness/quality of NNetNav-6K is unclear; the dataset differs from the training data, lacks experiments, and marginal improvements make its impact doubtful.
Lack of clarity on whether the reward LLM is applied to filter the instruction-first baseline.
Insufficient details on the use of the reward model and filtering of incorrect trajectories.
No error analysis or discussion of limitations.
Performance gains are minor for certain websites.
No comparison with previous methods that report results on the WebArena.
